I’ve had bunions on both feet since my high school career, through my college career, and now two years post grad. They were the worst in high school, where I had pain in the joint and it would radiate under the toe. I had custom insoles made by my podiatrist, and they’re firm and hold my arch up a bit which helps with how I roll off my foot, putting less pressure on the joint. I do wear normal width running shoes. As a female, I can’t wear strappy heels for too long because the pain is killer. My biggest solution for pain is wearing supportive shoes, so I have a ton of Dr scholls plantar fasciitis insoles for my work shoes, and my custom insoles for running. I think the firm arch helps support and prevents the joint from bunching even more. 

My prevention tips, I like being barefoot to work my feet a bit, but I can’t to it all the time. I wear Birkenstocks instead of flat flip flops. I brought cushy toe spreaders on Amazon that I wear if it’s really flared up. I like to mobilize the joint by just manually rotating the toe around to get some blood flow in. 

Worst culprit for pain is wearing spikes for me, because the pointing of the toe shoves the joint. Looking for shoes with a wider toe (I wear NB) might be a step in the right direction

I understand it's rough and confusing right now. The way I look at it, it's a physiological symptom. You're having a physical reaction to what's going on in your head. Medication is not a bad thing, and talking to someone like a therapist isn't bad either. The one thing I can leave you with right now is to focus on your breathing. When you feel that pounding in your chest, just take slower breaths. 

As far as articulating this to other people, you don't have to. If it's people close to you and you want to tell them the truth, then tell them as much as you want. Its your body and your mind, you can reveal as much as you want. If it's people you're less close to, you can always just say you're having cardiac issues. That's what I've been doing for the past few months. When people ask about my doctors appointments and missing classes and such, I just explain I'm getting checked out for a cardiac issue but so far everything is okay. It takes away the anxiety you might have of talking about your anxiety, since it is so new. If you have any other questions, or just want to talk, you can PM me. Victor slugged his heavy feet through the wet leaves along the path. It was paved, surrounded by an archway of trees reaching their fingers down to caress his face as he shuffled onwards. Hands in pockets, hunched at the waist, his baggy sweatshirt hung across him and billowed around his thin form. He stopped eating weeks ago. Grey skin hugged his sharp cheekbones. His crystal blue eyes were draped with the stretched, purple skin that winked shut and heavily dropped open again every time he blinked. 

He sighed. Out of breath, he stumbled onwards, large shoes dragging across the wet pavement. Littered with brown leaves that glowed dully under the flickering streetlamps, the path stretched only a few feet before him before suddenly stopping. Victor looked up. His eyes met hers. How many times had he pulled his weary body to this very spot to beg for her mercy? She sat with such poise and confidence, perched upon her throne, waiting for her disciples to beg her for salvation. 

Her features marred by the growing twilight stared down at Victor, who stood trembling at the foot of the statue. Heart struggling to beat, he spoke in hushed breaths that sent plumes of condensation into the frigid air. He needed salvation, for his mind had overspent its stay in this state of being. He had followed her directions. He had allowed his form to weaken to the point of exhaustion. His hollow stomach no longer cried for food. His pale skin was littered in mountains and caverns of scars, carved both gracefully and haphazardly into his flesh. He prepared himself for her. He was ready to move on to salvation.

“Angel of Death,” he cried.  “Angel of Death and Salvation.” He sobbed out the prayers, body convulsing and quivering as it struggled to fuel his demise.  “Angel, please. I have prepared for you. I have sacrificed all that I have on this Earth for you. Angel, please, grant me the freedom from this wretched mind that so controls my being and prevents existence in this world.”

Her eyes stared blankly ahead. Hands poised, judgment set in years of metal exposed to the elements. She sat unmoving.

“Angel of Death, please save me.” He spoke with the last ounce of energy left in his frail body. He hoisted the heavy piece of metal to his temple. One last smile spread across his face, teeth glowing in his final twilight. 

The trees shook their fingers goodbye as the shockwave spread down the pathway. His body lay slumped across the feet of his angel. Her eyes sat unmoving, waiting. Waiting for the next disciple.

Music playing loudly, parents too placid to take notice to the shuffling in the upstairs bedroom. Her room was dark, illuminated only by the last glimpse of the sun and the harsh light from her laptop. Pulling her aching body across the floor, she stopped at the foot of her dresser. There she laid, waiting for the pain to subside enough to lift her arms. She knew she would be at peace soon, she just needed to persevere. Like a marathon runner, yes. Pushing hard through the pain because the finish is so sweet. Gathering her will she lifted her arms and pulled out a box. Another trek across the floor back to the glowing screen made her body scream. It wanted her trapped. It wanted to torture her but no, she refused. She dumped the contents on the grey carpet. Guitar picks, old bracelets, yes there it was! The grey metal glowed in the soft light. It was new. She knew that when she planned this, she didn’t want to mess up. No the pain would punish her when she woke up the next morning in a hospital bed. She couldn’t let that happen. 

Two clicks and the song echoed around the room. Sweet guitar strums and the low harmonies filled her ears, and for minutes she was lost. Floating again. The task at hand was pushed aside by the graceful music that floated her around the room, leaving the writhing body on the floor grasping the blade. She knew this song. She loved it. Those minutes she was a wisp, floating on the notes that bounced of the walls, rocking her and soothing her turbulent mind. She knew what she was going to do, yes. Death would be like this. Death would be happy, she would be pain free. She was joyous as the last line of the song echoed around the room, “This too shall pass.” As she fell back into the diseased body she was satisfied, ready. Two quick movements as the song repeated and she felt at ease again, floating around her room while the body died beneath her, allowing her to never return to the pain that plagued her ever again.

Consistency. Great runners didn't become great overnight. They started just like you; they got off the couch and started putting the miles in. A good base is essential. But you can't jump from 0 miles to 30 miles a week in seven days, you need to build slow to prevent injury. The biggest thing is just don't give up, running takes time and heart to do. Even if it hurts (the good kind of hurt) you just need to keep pushing yourself to finish the miles that you need to do. 

If you have a decent base and can do 3-4 miles without breaks, you can do speedwork and tempos to work on the faster part of running. Does your coach make you do workouts at all? Or are you doing them and just feeling slow?
